source.title: Evaluating Representational Similarity Measures from the Lens of Functional Correspondence
source.authors: Yi-Qing Bo; Ansh K. Soni; Sudhanshu Srivastava; Meenakshi Khosla

page_placements.theme: Similarity predicts behavior or transfer only under particular metrics and conditions

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling; the full paper text, including appendices and references, is present.
record.tranche_reason: It compares multiple representational similarity measures and tests how their findings vary across behavioral datasets and analysis settings, addressing metric dependence with a different method from the original convergence hypothesis.
record.gate_note: The paper measures pairwise similarities among vision models and reports outcomes for multiple similarity measures, so these results bear on metric dependence (V6). It does not sweep model scale or performance, test image-caption alignment, or test seed convergence, interchangeability, or universal features.
record.test_reason: The study compares one pool of 19 ImageNet vision models (plus random versions) under 8 representational similarity measures. It shows that the model-to-model similarity structure, including how alike different architectures and trained versus untrained models look, changes strongly with the measure (cross-metric r=0.58). That bears directly on V6's claim that measured convergence depends on the metric. It does not sweep scale, modality, seeds, stitching or features, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors compare 8 representational metrics and conclude that geometry-preserving metrics (Procrustes, linear CKA, RSA) best separate trained from untrained models and best match behavior. Linear predictivity and CCA match behavior weakly. Representational metrics are far less mutually consistent than behavioral ones. Metric choice should follow behaviorally meaningful comparisons.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares several representational metrics on pretrained vision models and evaluates their relation to behavioral similarities. It does not test similarity growth with scale, cross-modal alignment, or the original convergence hypothesis directly.
record.method_sensitivity: Representational measure changes model separation and correspondence with behavioral measures. The study also checks intermediate versus penultimate layers and controls soft-matching feature dimensionality; these checks report high similarity across the tested settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Representational metrics differ in how well their model-similarity structure matches behavioral (error-pattern) similarity: Procrustes r=0.70, linear CKA 0.66, RSA 0.53, linear predictivity 0.30, CCA 0.22.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Geometry-preserving similarity measures track functional/behavioral similarity between models better than flexible mapping measures.

fits_no_version.finding: Behavioral metrics barely separate CNNs from transformers (best d′=0.61), suggesting behavioral convergence across architectures. This is a behavioral, not representational, result.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecturally different models trained on the same task converge in error structure.

record.problems: The authors note that the analysis focuses on coarse distinctions (trained versus untrained and CNNs versus transformers), not subtle architectural or initialization differences. Their d′ measure assumes Gaussian distributions and their Pearson correlations assume linearity. The paper describes 20 behavioral datasets but later states that model similarity matrices are averaged across 17 datasets; it also gives differing counts for representational measures in different sections.
record.rows_left_out: No additional distinct numerical outcomes bearing on V6 were extracted beyond the reported group-separation scores, cross-metric consistency, behavioral correspondence, layer check, and soft-matching dimensionality control. Behavioral-only measures and raw accuracy results were left out because they do not measure representational convergence.

untested.parts: No scale or capability sweep of cross-model alignment.
No vision–language or paired image–caption comparison.
No same-architecture, different-seed comparisons. The authors say initialization differences were not explored.
No stitching or mapping-loss evaluation. Linear predictivity is used only as a similarity score.
No interpretable feature or circuit matching.

It does not report how mutual k-NN similarity varies with k at the penultimate layer. It does not report how the magnitude of alignment changes between in-distribution and OOD inputs; the authors only say datasets are highly consistent.
No plateau analysis and no test of whether shared data or objectives cause alignment.

missing.what: Per-metric correlations between intermediate- and penultimate-layer similarity matrices, including mutual k-NN at k=10,20,50,100,200 (e.g. k-NN(10) 0.90 vs k-NN(200) 0.89 at depth 0.6). Each layer also has a cross-metric baseline mean of 0.72–0.74.
Per-metric d′ for architectural separation for metrics other than soft-matching, and the qualitative statement that linear predictivity shows no separation of architecture or training.

record.verdict_notes: This is a metric-validity study, not a convergence study. Its bearing on V6 comes mainly from the cross-metric disagreement (R5) and the contrasts between metrics (R1–R4). Count inconsistencies exist: 8 vs 9 representational measures, 9 vs 10 behavioral measures, and 20 vs 17 datasets. Mutual k-NN (the PRH metric) is included, but its own results are reported only in Table 1 and in appendix matrices.

versions.untested_parts: Whether alignment between independently trained models rises with model scale and capability.
Cross-modal alignment of vision and language models on paired images and captions as model quality changes.
Convergence across random initializations of the same architecture, including shared features or subspaces.
Whether representations can be mapped or stitched between models with little loss.
Whether interpretable features or circuits recur across models.

It compares representational measures and reports some layer and dimensionality checks, but does not systematically vary nearest-neighbour count or comprehensively test out-of-distribution choices as a cause of convergence disappearing.
Whether alignment plateaus or remains incomplete as models scale, and whether shared data or objectives explain alignment rather than a common model of reality.

conditions.value: intermediate layers sampled at normalized depth indices 0.6, 0.7, and 0.8 versus penultimate layer

rows.baseline: Different metrics at the same depth: r = 0.73 ± 0.006
rows.uncertainty: As reported in the mean and ± values
rows.locator: Layer Selection and Controlled Feature Extraction; Table 1

rows.check: For layer choice as a setting, model-similarity structure barely changes (intermediate vs penultimate r=0.86±0.003), so layer dependence is absent. relationships.condition: Choice of similarity measure, 19 ImageNet vision models, penultimate layer, across 17–20 datasets
relationships.reason: Similarity matrices from different metrics agree only moderately (r=0.58, R5). Trained/untrained separation ranges from d′=3.73 (Procrustes) to 0.55 (linear predictivity) (R1–R3). Architectural separation is metric-specific (R4).
relationships.display_finding: Similarity matrices agreed only moderately across metrics at r=0.58, while trained–untrained separation ranged from d′=3.73 for Procrustes to 0.55 for linear predictivity, and architectural separation also varied by metric.

tranche.reason: The study demonstrates metric-dependent representational similarity structure, qualifying convergence interpretations and directly bearing on the V6 challenge.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv v2 dated September 2025. Source counts vary: Figure 1 reports 9 representational/10 behavioral metrics, Discussion reports 8/9, and appendix matrices cover 17 datasets versus 20 overall; R5 is metric agreement, and R6–R10 measure metric–behavior correspondence rather than convergence.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Across the tested representational metrics and datasets
reader_labels.reason: Metric outcomes differ: Procrustes and soft-matching discriminate model groups strongly, while CCA and linear predictivity show lower trained-versus-untrained separation; their behavioral correspondences also vary (R1-R4, R6-R10).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Intermediate-layer comparisons and soft-matching after equalizing feature dimension
reader_labels.reason: The reported intermediate/penultimate matrix correlation is high, and equalizing dimensions leaves the soft-matching matrices highly correlated while preserving architectural separation (R11-R12); the paper does not show metric- or setting-dependent convergence always vanishing.
